meta.company: CoreWeave, Inc. Class A Common Stock
meta.subtitle: An AI cloud growing 112% a year on a $104 billion backlog, financed by a debt load whose interest already exceeds its operating profit

advisories: gate ceiling SELL (distress) — advisory, not applied

analystSentiment.commentary:
CoreWeave is a bet on the AI build-out priced through a balance sheet, and the two halves point in opposite directions. In the second quarter ended June 30, 2026 revenue was $2.6 billion, up 112% year over year, the revenue backlog reached $104 billion, and management raised its year-end power guidance; the market values the equity at ~$44.1B, and the Street, with 19 Buys against 10 Holds and 1 Sell, carries a consensus target of $141.41, +74.8% above the $80.92 price. That is the growth story, and it is real: the company rents NVIDIA infrastructure at scale on long committed contracts, and demand, in management's telling, exceeds supply.

The other half is the financing. FY25 total debt was $29.8B against total equity of $3.3B, FY25 free cash flow was -$7.3B, and interest expense, net in the quarter was $640 million, larger than any operating profit the company has produced; the quarter's operating loss was $49 million and the net loss $626 million. The model front-loads capital expenditure, guided to $11.5 billion to $13.5 billion in the third quarter alone, and repays it from contracted revenue that arrives later, so the equity's value turns on whether the backlog converts to cash before financing conditions or a large customer change.

We rate the shares HOLD with a target range of $70–$110. The probability-weighted fair value of $91.00 sits modestly above the price, but the distribution is unusually wide: a bull case that re-rates toward the Street on backlog execution, and a bear case in which leverage, customer concentration and the hyperscaler competition the July headlines flag take the equity well below its 52-week low. The consensus upside is offset by interest coverage of -0.3x, and the expected value does not justify adding at this price.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
CoreWeave, Inc. is a specialized cloud computing company headquartered in Livingston, New Jersey, that provides GPU-accelerated infrastructure for artificial-intelligence workloads. Originally incorporated in 2017 as Atlantic Crypto Corporation and renamed in December 2019, it went public in 2025, so its record as a listed company is short and its financial history spans only the three fiscal years the tables below cover. Management describes the business as The Essential Cloud for AI: a tightly integrated platform of NVIDIA GPU clusters, high-speed networking, AI-optimized storage, bare-metal control, and a software layer it calls Mission Control, sold mostly through committed contracts rather than on demand. The proxy puts the 2025 footprint at more than 850MW of active power across 43 data centers, and the second-quarter call put active power at 1.5 gigawatts, with a target of at least 8 gigawatts by 2030.

The company's economics are those of an infrastructure builder. Revenue comes from access to compute; cost of revenue is data-center rent, power and depreciation; and technology and infrastructure expense is dominated by depreciation of the servers and networking gear placed in service. The result is a company that is EBITDA-positive and deeply loss-making at the same time, because depreciation and interest on the debt that funds the fleet turn operating results into net losses.

The vendor gives no product breakdown, so its one revenue disaggregation is geographic, and the moat section reads it as the segment mix: the United States was 93.6% of FY25 revenue and Non-US 6.4%. Customers named on the call span AI labs and enterprises, from Caterpillar and Isomorphic Labs to Flow Traders, IMC and, through CoreWeave Federal, Leidos. NVIDIA is both the company's key supplier and, per the proxy, a 10.66% holder of its Class A stock.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body:
The thesis is that CoreWeave's equity is a levered call on the AI capital-expenditure cycle, and the disclosures let us size the call but not price the strike. What is verifiable is the demand: revenue up 112% in the quarter, a backlog of $104 billion up 246% year over year, more than $25 billion of net new commitments added early in the third quarter, and a raised year-end power target. What is equally verifiable is the cost of carrying it: $29.8B of FY25 debt against $3.3B of equity, free cash flow of -$7.3B, and interest expense that now exceeds operating income. The company funds a capital program measured in tens of billions with debt, convertibles and equity, repaying it from contracts that pay out over five years.

We rate the shares HOLD. The bull's case is the backlog and the margin inflection management says began this quarter; the bear's case is that the equity is thin against the debt, that a limited number of customers drive the revenue, and that the July headlines show hyperscalers, Meta among them, weighing entry into the same market. The stock has already fallen from a 52-week high of $153.20 to $80.92, which prices in some of that risk. At the current price the probability-weighted value is only modestly positive, and the downside tail is a permanent impairment of equity, not a drawdown.

catalysts: Margin inflection: management guided a low-teens adjusted operating margin by the fourth quarter, and the financials and growth sections carry what would confirm it.
Backlog conversion: the contracted backlog and the net new third-quarter commitments turn into revenue as capacity is delivered; the growth section carries the ramp.
The July pricing action: management raised prices across its SKUs after the quarter, which lands in the second half and is not yet in reported margins.
International expansion: power contracted outside the U.S., including in Indonesia, opens the Non-US line the moat section describes.
Financing terms: management has cut its cost of debt, and any further improvement eases the interest burden the balance-sheet section carries.
risks: Leverage: debt many times equity, with interest expense already above operating income; the balance-sheet section carries the mechanism.
Cash burn and capital need: negative free cash flow and a capital program larger than operating cash flow require continual access to capital, which the 10-Q names as a risk.
Customer concentration: the 10-Q states a limited number of customers drive a substantial portion of revenue, so the loss of one would be material; the risk section carries it.
Hyperscaler competition: the July headlines are dominated by reports that Meta plans an AI cloud business, which brokers split over; the risk section carries the overhang.
Control: a multi-class structure concentrates voting power with the Co-Founders, and the management section carries what that limits.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The income statement is a growth company's, layered over a lender's. Revenue rose from $0.2B in FY23 to $1.9B in FY24 and $5.1B in FY25, growth of +736.6% then +167.9%, and the second quarter added another {+ +112% +} to $2,575 million from $1,212 million a year earlier, with management attributing roughly 93% of the increase to expansion within the existing customer base. Gross margin has held in a band, 70.0% in FY23, 74.2% in FY24 and 71.7% in FY25, so the platform sells at a healthy contribution level. The problem sits below gross profit. Operating margin swung from -6.3% in FY23 to +16.9% in FY24 and back to -0.9% in FY25, and the quarter posted an operating loss of $49 million against a $19 million profit a year earlier, because the two cost lines that scale with the fleet climbed sharply: cost of revenue rose 181% to $879 million, 34% of revenue against 26%, on rent up approximately $335 million and power up approximately $87 million, and technology and infrastructure expense rose 125% to $1,507 million on depreciation that increased approximately $752 million, from $537 million to approximately $1.3 billion.

Below the operating line the debt takes over. Interest expense, net was $640 million in the quarter, up 140% from $267 million, and it turned a small operating loss into a net loss of $626 million, against $290 million a year earlier; a $125 million other-income item partly offset it. EBITDA, by contrast, was positive and rising, -$0.4B, $0.5B and $2.5B across the three years, which is why the trailing EV/EBITDA of 35.2x is a real multiple where the -22.3x P/E is not. Net income was -$0.6B, -$0.9B and -$1.2B, and diluted EPS -1.47, -2.33 and -2.81, the loss widening as the capital base grew. The line to watch is not revenue, which is compounding, but whether operating income can climb above the interest bill.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet is the reason this is a HOLD. Total debt grew from $2.0B in FY23 to $10.6B in FY24 and $29.8B in FY25, net debt from $1.8B to $9.3B to $25.9B, while total equity was negative in FY23 and FY24 and reached only $3.3B in FY25 after the IPO. Trailing net debt to EBITDA is 17.7x and interest coverage is -0.3x, and the current ratio has sat below one throughout, 0.50, 0.39 and 0.46, so current liabilities exceed current assets by a wide margin. This is a company financing long-lived assets with a large and fast-growing debt stack, and the highlight cells chosen show it plainly.

Management's framing is that the leverage is asset-level and self-liquidating: a five-year contract's capital cost is front-loaded and funded with debt, customer prepayments and corporate capital, and the debt is repaid from the contracted revenue before the cluster comes off contract. On the call the company reported more than $6.9 billion in cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities at quarter end, approximately $18 billion raised in the quarter across debt, convertibles and equity, more than $32 billion of debt and equity capital secured to date, and a weighted average cost of debt reduced by almost 300 basis points, worth approximately $1.1 billion of annualized interest saving. The case rests on that machine continuing to turn; the risk is that it depends on open capital markets and on the backlog paying as underwritten, neither of which the pack can guarantee.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow shows why the debt keeps growing. Operating cash flow is positive and rising, $1.8B, $2.7B and $3.1B across FY23 to FY25, but capital expenditure dwarfs it, -$2.9B, -$8.7B and -$10.3B, so free cash flow was -$1.1B, -$6.0B and -$7.3B, free-cash-flow margins of -485.0%, -310.8% and -141.3%. The margin improving toward zero is the one favorable trend in the series: the burn is shrinking relative to revenue even as it grows in dollars. There are no buybacks and no dividends, which is correct for a company at this stage.

The gap between operating cash flow and capital expenditure is filled with financing, and the guidance makes the scale explicit: capital expenditure of $11.5 billion to $13.5 billion in the third quarter alone, more than the whole of the prior fiscal year's outlay. Management's argument is that this spending is contracted against the $104 billion backlog and underwritten to a return before a contract is signed, and that as clusters come off their initial term the company can recontract them with no asset-level debt remaining. The judgment on cash is that the model can work, and that it cannot self-fund at this pace: every quarter of this capital program requires new capital, and the terms of that capital, which the improving cost of debt has helped, are as important to the equity as the revenue line.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
CoreWeave cannot be valued on earnings, and the multiples say why. The trailing P/E of -22.3x and the forward P/E of -20.2x are negative because consensus expects losses through FY27E, with EPS of -$4.01 in FY26E and -$1.97 in FY27E. What is left is revenue and EBITDA. Price to sales is 5.8x and trailing EV/EBITDA is 35.2x, a rich multiple that only makes sense against the growth: consensus revenue of $12.9B in FY26E and $26.5B in FY27E would roughly double the base twice, and the FY26E figure is +152% on FY25. The market is paying for a revenue line it expects to compound, not for current profit, and peers are pending a peer data source, so we cannot place the multiple against the neocloud group.

The Street is constructive and widely spread: 30 analysts, 19 Buys, 10 Holds and 1 Sell, with a consensus target of $141.41 (+74.8%), a median of $150.00 and a range of $74.00–$192.00. That range, from below the current price to more than double it, is the honest picture of a stock whose value depends on assumptions the disclosures cannot settle. The shares sit at $80.92 against a 52-week range of $60.55 – $153.20, roughly a fifth of the way up it. Our view is that the consensus embeds continued open capital markets and uninterrupted customer spend, and that the market's own price, set after the July competition scare, better reflects the balance of a compounding backlog against a levered balance sheet.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The backlog converts and margins inflect as guided: adjusted operating income reaches a low-teens margin by the fourth quarter, the July price increase and the higher-margin inference and software lines lift the mix, capital markets stay open, and the shares re-rate to the Street's median target of $150.00 as CoreWeave is seen to grow into its debt.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue compounds toward the $12.9B FY26E consensus and beyond, but the market keeps a discount for the leverage, the customer concentration and the competition overhang, so the shares hold near the current price while losses continue and the balance sheet grows; the stock stays roughly where it is at $85.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Financing tightens or a large customer reduces its commitment, the capital program measured in tens of billions cannot be funded on acceptable terms, or hyperscaler competition compresses pricing; the thin equity absorbs the leverage and the shares fall through the 52-week low toward $40 as the market re-prices the risk of permanent impairment.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 40% and split the rest evenly between the Bull at $150 and the Bear at $40, for a probability-weighted fair value of $91.00, modestly above the price and inside the HOLD envelope; the $70–$110 target range brackets the Base. The Bull case takes the Street's median rather than its high, because even the midpoint asks the reader to believe the margin inflection holds, the capital keeps flowing and the competition stays off. The Base case is the market's current price with the ramp delivered, because the backlog supports the revenue but the balance sheet caps the multiple. The Bear case carries nearly a third of the weight, and its implied price sits below the 52-week low, because the downside here is not a drawdown but a permanent loss of equity: a company with interest coverage of -0.3x and $29.8B of debt has little cushion if the capital markets it depends on close.

A move to BUY would need the fourth-quarter margin inflection to print and free cash flow to turn toward break-even at scale, or the debt to be visibly self-liquidating as contracts pay down. A move to SELL would follow a failed or dilutive financing, a cut to the backlog or guidance, or evidence that a major customer is reducing its spend.

segments.name: UNITED STATES
segments.body: The vendor gives no product breakdown for CoreWeave, so the one revenue disaggregation is geographic, and the United States was 93.6% of FY25 revenue, $4.8B. This is the installed base: the data centers, the 1.5 gigawatts of active power the call reported, and the customer roster management named, from Caterpillar's Vera Rubin deployment to Isomorphic Labs, the systematic trading firms Flow Traders and IMC, and Leidos through CoreWeave Federal. The concentration is the point and the risk: almost all revenue is domestic, and the 10-Q states that a limited number of customers drive a substantial portion of it, so the segment is both the company's strength, a dense book of long committed contracts, and its exposure, since the loss of one major customer would be felt across the whole line. The moat here is the scarcity of energized, production-grade GPU capacity at scale, which the company has and new entrants cannot conjure quickly; the counter is that the capacity runs on NVIDIA silicon its major customers can also buy.

segments.name: Non-US
segments.body: Non-US revenue was 6.4% of the FY25 total, $330M, and it is the growth vector rather than the base. On the call management said it has contracted more than one gigawatt of power outside the United States and is entering the APAC region with 360 megawatts in Indonesia that begins coming online in approximately 18 months, and it expects international markets to become a major driver of growth as it follows customers into their own geographies. The strategic logic is the same as at home, securing power and sites ahead of demand, but the execution risk is higher: new jurisdictions bring their own power markets, regulators and currencies, and the revenue is years out. For now the segment is small enough that it changes the growth story more than the current numbers, and it is one of the few parts of the business where the company is building capacity it has not yet contracted at scale.

moatFactors.name: Power and capacity at scale
moatFactors.body: Access to energized capacity is the scarce input in AI infrastructure, and CoreWeave has assembled it quickly: nearly 500 megawatts of active power added in the quarter alone, on the way to a target of at least 8 gigawatts by 2030, with management noting it added more power in the quarter than any single competing neocloud operates in total. It reports being first to validate NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72. The counter is that power is procured from utilities and third parties whose limits the 10-Q lists first among its risks, so the advantage is a lead in securing a shared input, not ownership of it.

moatFactors.name: Contracted backlog and switching costs
moatFactors.body: The business is built on long committed contracts, and the backlog reached $104 billion, up 246% year over year, with more than $25 billion of net new commitments added early in the third quarter and roughly 93% of the quarter's revenue growth coming from existing customers expanding. Five-year committed contracts and the cost of migrating a running AI workload create real switching costs. The counter is concentration: the same contract structure that locks customers in means a limited number of them carry the book, so the backlog's quality depends on a handful of counterparties continuing to pay and to grow.

moatFactors.name: Software and platform depth
moatFactors.body: CoreWeave sells more than raw GPUs: a software layer it calls Mission Control, plus storage, CPU, networking and managed services that together exceed $400 million of annual recurring revenue, and a managed inference platform whose booked ARR grew from $1 million to more than $100 million and is guided to at least $250 million by the end of 2026. These higher-margin lines are the path off pure hardware resale. The counter is that the underlying compute is NVIDIA silicon, and the hyperscalers the July headlines name have their own software stacks and can integrate the same chips, so the software depth narrows the gap rather than closing it.

moatFactors.name: Customers who can become competitors
moatFactors.body: The structural weakness is that CoreWeave's market can be entered by its own suppliers and customers. The risk section details the July headlines in which Meta is reported weighing exactly this, and NVIDIA is at once the key supplier and a 10.66% shareholder. The 10-Q names intense competition and the risk that hyperscalers compete directly. Management's answer is that demand exceeds supply and that scarce, energized capacity in production is itself the moat; the market's answer, in the stock's fall from its high, is that the moat may not hold if the major buyers build their own.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow: real but contestable. What is durable is the lead in energized capacity and the book of five-year contracts, which take time and capital to replicate and which give the revenue visibility the backlog quantifies. What is not durable on its own is the technical layer, because it sits on NVIDIA hardware that CoreWeave's major customers can buy directly, and the competitive position, because those customers and the hyperscalers can enter the market, as the July headlines show they are considering. The widening path is the shift toward software, inference and international capacity, higher-margin and stickier than raw GPU rental; the narrowing path is a demand environment in which compute stops being scarce, at which point a levered reseller of other companies' chips has little to fall back on. We rate the moat narrow because the scarcity that protects it today is a function of an AI capital cycle that the company does not control and cannot guarantee will persist.

points: Revenue is compounding from a small base: up +736.6% in FY24 and +167.9% in FY25 to $5.1B, and up 112% in the second quarter to $2.6B, with management raising its year-end power guidance. The counter is that management itself warns recent growth may not be indicative of future growth.

The backlog gives the revenue visibility: $104 billion at quarter end, up 246% year over year, plus more than $25 billion of net new commitments early in the third quarter; consensus has revenue reaching $26.5B in FY27E. The counter is that converting backlog requires the capital program the risk section describes.

Margins are guided to inflect: adjusted operating income of $128 million in the quarter, guided to $200 million to $260 million in the third and a low-teens margin by the fourth, helped by an approximately 25% July price increase and by contracts signed at contribution margins 5 to 10 percentage points above recent ones. The counter is that interest expense is guided to $860 million to $940 million in the third quarter, still far above operating income.

Higher-margin lines are scaling: products beyond GPUs exceed $400 million of ARR, and managed inference grew from $1 million to more than $100 million of booked ARR, guided to at least $250 million by year end. These diversify a business that is otherwise GPU rental.

Power is the gating input and the plan is explicit: 1.5 gigawatts active, guided above 1.85 gigawatts by year end and at least 8 gigawatts by 2030, with more than one gigawatt contracted outside the U.S. The counter is that each gigawatt requires capital and power the company must secure from others.

The growth is bought, not earned in cash: capital expenditure is guided to $11.5 billion to $13.5 billion in the third quarter alone, so the pace of revenue is set by how much capacity the company can fund and deliver, which ties the growth rate to the debt markets.

management.leadership: CoreWeave is led by its three Co-Founders and a hired finance chief: Michael Intrator is Chief Executive Officer and President, Brian Venturo is Chief Strategy Officer, Brannin McBee is Chief Development Officer, Nitin Agrawal is Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer, and Jonathan Jones is Chief Revenue Officer. The April 2026 proxy, the company's first as a public company, states that the board has six directors and that all but Intrator and Venturo qualify as independent, the two being non-independent as employees. On execution the team has done what it said it would at speed: taking the company public in 2025, scaling revenue to $5.1B, reaching 1.5 gigawatts of active power, and raising capital at a pace few companies its age have matched. The reservation is that this is a young public company with a short reporting history and a strategy that depends on continuous access to capital, so the market has not yet seen how the team operates through a tighter financing environment, which is the test that matters most for a business built on debt.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is dominated by one decision, made every quarter: how much capacity to build and how to fund it. The company is deploying capital expenditure guided to $11.5 billion to $13.5 billion in the third quarter alone, far in excess of the $3.1B of operating cash flow it generated in all of FY25, so the difference is financed, and management has raised it in size and variety, more than $32 billion of debt and equity capital secured to date, approximately $18 billion in the quarter alone across debt, convertibles and equity, including an inaugural Eurobond and a delayed-draw term loan backed by infrastructure. It has also worked the cost of that capital down, reducing its weighted average cost of debt by almost 300 basis points for roughly $1.1 billion of annualized interest saving. There are no buybacks or dividends, which is right. The judgment is that management is allocating coherently to a single thesis, growth through contracted capacity, and that the strategy has no margin for error: with interest coverage negative and equity thin, the company must keep raising capital on improving terms, and a single failed or dilutive financing would undo much of the progress the lower cost of debt has bought.
management.governance: The proxy is the April 22, 2026 statement, and the governance headline is control. CoreWeave has a multi-class structure in which Class A carries one vote and Class B ten, and the 10-Q lists the concentration of voting power with the Co-Founders among its risk factors. The compensation framework reads conventionally for a newly public company: a compensation committee of independent directors, an independent advisor in Semler Brossy, stock ownership guidelines, a clawback policy, double-trigger change-in-control terms and no tax gross-ups. The excerpt carries the philosophy and the practices but no pay tables or say-on-pay result, so we make no claim on quantum. One related-party arrangement stands out: Equity Exchange Right Agreements entered in September 2024 let each Co-Founder require the company to exchange Class A shares received on equity awards for Class B shares, covering 7,214,460 Class A shares as of March 31, 2026, a mechanism that preserves the founders' high-vote position as their awards settle. Governance here is founder-controlled by design, and a minority shareholder should price that in rather than expect to influence outcomes.
management.insiderOwnership: Ownership, as of April 15, 2026, is concentrated in the founders through Class B stock. Percentages rest on 442,969,348 Class A and 99,997,704 Class B shares. Michael Intrator holds 1.19% of Class A but 54.93% of Class B, for 38.70% of total voting power; Brian Venturo holds 28.89% of Class B and 20.30% of the vote; Brannin McBee holds 20.96% of Class B and 14.59% of the vote. All executive officers and directors as a group, 12 people, hold 5.38% of Class A and 100.00% of Class B, for 72.32% of total voting power. Among outside holders of Class A, funds managed by Magnetar Financial hold 17.07%, NVIDIA Corporation 10.66% and Jane Street Group 6.53%. The pattern is a company controlled by its founders through super-voting stock, with a strategically important supplier, NVIDIA, holding a meaningful economic stake. Public shareholders own most of the economics and little of the control, and no insider transaction data is in the captured record.

idiosyncratic: Leverage and the interest bill. FY25 total debt was $29.8B against $3.3B of equity, trailing net debt to EBITDA is 17.7x, interest coverage is -0.3x, and interest expense, net was $640 million in the quarter, above any operating profit the company earns. The model treats this debt as asset-level and self-liquidating, but that holds only if the contracted revenue pays as underwritten and the capital markets stay open; if either fails, the equity, which is thin, absorbs the shortfall.

The capital treadmill. Free cash flow was -$7.3B in FY25 and capital expenditure is guided to $11.5 billion to $13.5 billion in the third quarter alone, so the company cannot self-fund its growth and must keep raising capital, which the 10-Q names as a risk. Management has lowered its cost of debt, but a single failed, delayed or dilutive financing would slow the build-out and pressure the equity.

Customer concentration. The 10-Q states that a substantial portion of revenue is driven by a limited number of customers, so the loss of, or a material reduction in spending from, one or a few of its major customers would hit revenue and the backlog directly. The five-year contract structure mitigates near-term churn but concentrates the risk in a few counterparties.

Hyperscaler competition. The July 1-2 headlines are dominated by reports that Meta is weighing an AI cloud business, and brokers split on whether it matters. The concern is structural: CoreWeave's major customers and its key supplier can enter its market, and if compute stops being scarce the pricing power management describes would erode.

Concentration of control and NVIDIA dependence. The multi-class structure concentrates the vote in insiders, whose executive-officer-and-director group holds the entire high-vote class, so public holders cannot influence outcomes, and the business depends on NVIDIA for the silicon it rents, a supplier that is also a 10.66% shareholder, aligning interests but concentrating dependence.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposure is the AI capital-expenditure cycle and the financing conditions that fuel it. CoreWeave's demand, its backlog and its pricing power all rest on enterprises and AI labs continuing to spend heavily on training and inference; management's view is that demand exceeds supply and will for years, but the company concedes that the adoption and pace of AI are inherently uncertain and that its recent growth may not persist. The financing side is the second channel: a business that funds a capital program of this size with debt and equity is directly exposed to credit spreads and equity appetite, and management noted pricing one recent term loan during a dislocated week for credit. The mechanism runs both ways: an AI spending boom validates the backlog and the leverage, while a slowdown in AI investment or a tightening in capital markets would hit revenue growth and refinancing at the same time, which for a company with negative interest coverage is the more dangerous combination. Power availability is the third systemic input, a shared grid constraint the company competes for alongside every other data-center builder.

body: **HOLD, target range $70–$110.** CoreWeave is growing revenue 112% a year, with a $104 billion backlog and its year-end power guidance raised, and it is also carrying far more debt than equity, with interest expense that already exceeds its operating income. Those two facts do not net to a clear buy or sell; they net to a wide distribution of outcomes, and a probability-weighted fair value of $91.00 that sits only modestly above the price.

What we would pay for is proof that the machine self-funds: the fourth-quarter margin inflection management guided, free cash flow turning toward break-even at scale, and the asset-level debt visibly paying down as contracts mature. What we cannot yet see is whether the capital markets stay open long enough and whether the major customers keep buying rather than building, and the July competition scare shows the market shares that doubt. Until the balance sheet stops growing faster than the equity can support, the risk-reward is balanced with a heavy downside tail.

We would move to BUY on a demonstrated path to positive free cash flow and self-liquidating leverage, or on the margin inflection landing as guided; we would move to SELL on a failed or heavily dilutive financing, a cut to the backlog or guidance, or evidence that a major customer is reducing its commitment.
